extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (Schopenhauer/Metaphysics); scholars of ethics and metaphysics
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading of a philosophical treatise (excerpt from Schopenhauer's The World as Will and Representation) discussing Stoic ethics, the distinction of will and idea, and limits of scientific explanation. Useful for analysis, commentary, or pedagogy in metaphysics and ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish what depends on us and what does not
rubrics_metrics.description: “we should consider well and distinguish what depends upon us and what does not, and therefore entirely avoid counting upon the latter, whereby we shall certainly remain free from all pain, sorrow, and anxiety. But that which alone is dependent upon us is the will.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core Stoic kernel: attend only to what is within our control (the will) and avoid reliance on externals. Anti-pattern: counting on externals leads to pain, sorrow, and anxiety. Surrounding discussion notes disputes about applying terms bonum/malum to inner vs outer goods but treats the distinction as the operative ethical rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live in harmony with oneself (Zeno)
rubrics_metrics.description: Zeno’s ethical principle: for the attainment of the highest good one must live in harmony with oneself (consonanter vivere), i.e., determine oneself entirely rationally according to concepts, not according to changing impressions and moods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: set maxims (rules of conduct) as the aim rather than consequences or outward circumstances to achieve consistency. Emphasises rational self-determination and principled consistency rather than contingent feelings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live in harmony with nature (Kleanthes/Chrysippus)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Stoic addition: to live in harmony with nature (ὁμολογουμενως τῃ φυσει ζῃν); Kleanthes understood this as harmony with all nature, Chrysippus as harmony with human nature in particular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives material content to the formal rule of living in harmony with oneself. Implication: what accords with human nature (virtue) is the proper good, whereas satisfaction of animal desires accords with animal nature. Note tension in interpretation depending on whether 'nature' is taken broadly or human-specifically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue as the ethical aim (Stoic doctrine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stoic ethical system reduced to a doctrine of virtue: virtue is what alone is adapted to human nature and is the proper ethical aim; externals are indifferent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextual notes: Stoics sought unity of principle (ethics grounded in physics/theology). Critical observation in the text: the Stoic ideal can produce paradoxes (e.g., recommending suicide in incurable suffering), revealing tensions in making virtue the sole aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of mathematics and etiological (scientific) explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics treats ideas only as quantities (how-many/how-much); morphology and etiology (natural science) enumerate forms and causal laws but cannot reveal the inner nature or significance of phenomena ('the force of nature' remains unexplained).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological guidance: these disciplines supply form, order, and law but leave 'inner nature' and significance unanswered. Anti-pattern: assuming causal or quantitative explanation suffices to disclose the intrinsic meaning of perceived phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body as the objectivity of the will (identity of will and body)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thesis: 'The action of the body is nothing but the act of the will objectified' — the body is the objectivity of the will; acts of will and bodily movements are identical though given differently to consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: every genuine act of will is immediately a bodily movement; impressions on the body affect the will as pain or pleasure. Epistemological note: knowledge of the will is immediate and of a different order than knowledge of ideas; this is called a kind of 'philosophical truth' distinct from logical/empirical truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double knowledge creates individuality
rubrics_metrics.description: Because we know our body both as idea (object among objects) and immediately as will, this double, heterogeneous knowledge is what makes the knowing subject an individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: the special relation to one body yields individual perspective (I can 'be one' while 'know all'); methodological move: use analogy from one’s body (double knowledge) to judge whether external objects might likewise be manifestations of will. The text contrasts this with 'theoretical egoism' and treats the double knowledge as foundational for philosophical inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Will is immediate, groundless, and not fully determined by motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Motives determine only specific manifestations of will at particular times; the inner nature of the will itself lies outside the law of motivation and is 'groundless' (not fully explainable by motives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: motives are occasions for the will's appearance but do not explain why the will prefers one general course over another. Philosophical cross-reference: invokes Kant’s empirical vs intelligible character; promises fuller discussion in later books. Anti-pattern: treating motives as providing complete metaphysical account of volition.
